# 7.1 Regression trees {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The model

Partition the feature space into $M$ regions and predict a constant in each:

$$\hat f(x) = \sum_m c_m \mathbb{1}\{x \in R_m\}$$

Under squared loss the optimal constant is the region mean:

$$\hat c_m = \operatorname{ave}(y_i \mid x_i \in R_m)$$

::: {.check}
A tree is a step function. That is the whole model.
:::

## Greedy splitting

Finding the optimal partition is computationally infeasible, so we proceed **greedily**. At each
node, search over splitting variable $j$ and split point $s$:

$$\min_{j,s}\ \Big[ \min_{c_1}\sum_{x_i \in R_1(j,s)}(y_i - c_1)^2 + \min_{c_2}\sum_{x_i \in R_2(j,s)}(y_i - c_2)^2 \Big]$$

with $R_1(j,s) = \{x : x_j \le s\}$, $R_2(j,s) = \{x: x_j > s\}$.

::: {.muted}
The inner minimisations are just means, so one scan over sorted values of each feature suffices:
$O(p\, n \log n)$ per node.
:::

## Impurity, for classification

Replace variance with a measure on the node class proportions $\hat p_{mk}$:

$$\text{Gini} = \sum_{k} \hat p_{mk}(1-\hat p_{mk}), \qquad
\text{Entropy} = -\sum_k \hat p_{mk}\log \hat p_{mk}$$

$$\text{Misclassification} = 1 - \max_k \hat p_{mk}$$

## Which to grow with

Gini and entropy are differentiable and strictly concave, so they reward splits producing *purer*
nodes **even when the majority class does not change**.

::: {.warn}
Misclassification error is insensitive to that and makes a poor **growing** criterion — though it is
the right criterion for **pruning**.
:::

# 7.2 Cost-complexity pruning {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Grow, then cut back

Grow a large tree $T_0$, then choose a subtree minimising

$$C_\gamma(T) = \sum_{m=1}^{|T|} \sum_{x_i \in R_m}(y_i - \hat c_m)^2 + \gamma|T|$$

## Weakest-link pruning

As $\gamma$ increases from 0, the sequence of optimal subtrees is **nested**, obtained by
successively collapsing the internal node with the smallest per-leaf increase in error.

That gives a **one-dimensional family** indexed by $\gamma$ — selected by cross-validation, exactly
as we selected $\lambda$ in Session 05.

::: {.check}
The structural parallel is worth noticing: *every* method in this course has a complexity dial and a
CV procedure for setting it.
:::

# 7.3 Bagging {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The variance argument

Average $B$ trees fitted on bootstrap samples. If each has variance $\sigma^2$ and any two have
correlation $\rho$:

$$\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_b \hat f_b\Big) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2
\;\xrightarrow[B\to\infty]{}\; \rho\sigma^2$$

## Read that limit

Increasing $B$ kills the second term but leaves $\rho\sigma^2$ **untouched**.

::: {.check}
**This is the entire motivation for random forests.**
:::

If one predictor is strongly dominant, every bagged tree splits on it first and the trees are nearly
identical: $\rho \approx 1$, and bagging buys almost nothing.

## Random forests decorrelate

Restrict each split to a random subset of $m$ features.

::: {.tight}
- $m = \lfloor \sqrt p \rfloor$ for classification
- $m = \lfloor p/3\rfloor$ for regression
:::

Lower $m$ lowers $\rho$ but **raises individual-tree bias** — a bias–variance tradeoff *within* the
ensemble, tuned by CV.

## Out-of-bag error, free

Each observation is out-of-bag for roughly

$$(1 - 1/n)^n \to e^{-1} \approx 36.8\%$$

of trees, so the **OOB error** approximates CV error at no extra cost.

::: {.warn}
On a panel it is still optimistic — the omitted rows include other years of the same country.
Group-aware CV remains the honest number.
:::

# 7.4 Gradient boosting {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Functional gradient descent

Instead of averaging independent trees, build them **sequentially**, each correcting its
predecessor.

Think of minimising $\sum_i L(y_i, F(x_i))$ over the *function* $F$, by gradient descent **in
function space**.

## The pseudo-residual

At stage $m$, the negative gradient at the current fit:

$$r_{im} = -\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F = F_{m-1}}$$

::: {.tight}
- **Squared loss:** $r_{im} = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$ — literally the residual
- **Logistic loss:** $r_{im} = y_i - p_{m-1}(x_i)$ — the same probability residual as Session 06
:::

## The update

Fit a small tree $h_m$ to the pseudo-residuals:

$$F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu\, \gamma_m h_m(x), \qquad 0 < \nu \le 1$$

::: {.check}
The **shrinkage** $\nu$ is essential: small $\nu$ (0.01–0.1) with many trees generalises far better
than large $\nu$ with few. Halving $\nu$ roughly doubles the required $M$.
:::

## Three interacting knobs

| Knob | Controls |
|---|---|
| $\nu$ | learning rate — smaller generalises better |
| $M$ | number of trees — **too many overfits**, unlike a forest |
| $d$ | tree depth — maximum interaction order: $d=1$ additive, $d=2$ two-way |

::: {.warn}
A random forest does not overfit as you add trees. **A boosted model does.** The stopping point must
be chosen on validation data.
:::

## What XGBoost and LightGBM add

A second-order expansion and an explicit penalty:

$$\mathcal{L}^{(m)} \approx \sum_i \Big[g_i h_m(x_i) + \tfrac12 h_i h_m(x_i)^2\Big] + \Omega(h_m)$$

$$\Omega(h) = \gamma |T| + \tfrac12 \lambda \|w\|^2$$

Solving for the optimal leaf weights gives

$$w_j^\star = -\frac{G_j}{H_j+\lambda}$$

::: {.check}
Regularisation reappearing, in a third guise.
:::

# 7.5 Recovering interpretation {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The five tools

| Method | What it answers |
|---|---|
| Impurity importance | how often and how usefully a feature was split on |
| **Permutation importance** | how much test error rises when the feature is scrambled |
| Partial dependence | average marginal relationship |
| ICE curves | the per-observation version of a PDP |
| **SHAP** | additive attribution per prediction, from cooperative game theory |

## And their caveats

| Method | Caveat |
|---|---|
| Impurity importance | Biased toward high-cardinality features; computed **in-sample** |
| **Permutation importance** | **Breaks down under correlated features** — creates impossible data points |
| Partial dependence | Assumes $x_S \perp x_C$; hides heterogeneity |
| ICE curves | Reveals the heterogeneity a PDP averages away |
| **SHAP** | Unique under efficiency/symmetry/dummy/additivity; costly; assumes a value function |

## The honest summary

> These tools describe the **model**, not the world.

::: {.warn}
A large SHAP value means the model **relies on** that feature — not that the feature **causes** the
outcome.
:::

::: {.check}
Session 10 is where we finally take causality seriously. Until then, every sentence you write is
about prediction.
:::

# The lab {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Fit a pruned tree, a forest and a boosted model on your angle, under grouped CV
2. Compare against the Session 03 linear specification — does flexibility pay?
3. Produce **permutation** importance, never impurity importance
4. Draw one PDP and one set of ICE curves; describe the shapes in words
:::

::: {.warn}
Report the tuning you did and on which folds. A boosted model tuned and evaluated on one split is
reporting training error.
:::

## The two-minute report

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the models, the CV scheme, the baseline they beat
2. **The number** — error in the units of the outcome
3. **The catch** — that every statement is about prediction, not effect
:::

Full brief: [`02-lab/README.md`](02-lab/README.md)
:::
